references.text: The preceding verse in the parable of the dishonest manager, where the first debtor has his debt reduced. Verse 7 continues the pattern with another debtor whose debt is reduced from a hundred cors of wheat to eighty ([ref:Luk 16:6|Luke 16:6]).

A cor (κόρος) was a Hebrew unit of measure for dry goods. Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand cors of wheat as provisions, which shows the great value of wheat measured in cors ([ref:1 Kong 5:11|1 Kings 5:11]).
Another reference to the cor as a unit of measure for wheat, where Solomon promises large amounts of wheat and barley to Hiram's woodcutters ([ref:2 Krøn 2:10|2 Chronicles 2:10]).
The cor as a unit of measure for wheat is mentioned in connection with taxes that were paid, highlighting the economic value of wheat measured in cors ([ref:2 Krøn 27:5|2 Chronicles 27:5]).

Ezekiel mentions the cor as a unit of measure for wheat and oil in connection with dues and offerings, providing background for understanding the amount mentioned in the parable ([ref:Esek 45:13-14|Ezekiel 45:13-14]).

The introduction to the parable of the dishonest manager, where a rich man accuses the manager of wasting his property. Verse 7 shows how the manager acts wisely to secure his own future ([ref:Luk 16:1-2|Luke 16:1-2]).

The Lord's comment on the manager's actions – he praises the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. The action in verse 7 (reducing the debt) is the basis for this praise ([ref:Luk 16:8-9|Luke 16:8-9]).

Jesus speaks about the faithful and wise manager, which stands in contrast to the dishonest manager in chapter 16, but both texts deal with stewardship of a master's possessions ([ref:Luk 12:42|Luke 12:42]).
